items.prompt: After a user uploads a photo, three thumbnails must be generated and followers notified; the upload request must return in under 200 ms.
items.why: Work the user doesn't wait for, plus fan-out to several actions → publish an event and let workers process it asynchronously.

items.prompt: Clickstream events must feed a real-time dashboard computing per-minute counts per page, with late events handled correctly.
items.why: Windowed aggregation over events in motion is stream processing. The log only transports the events.

items.prompt: An order service must call payment, inventory and shipping; teams argue whether these should be REST calls or events, and how to roll back a failed step.
items.why: The question is service-to-service communication style and cross-service workflows (sagas) → the microservices topic. A queue is only one ingredient.

items.prompt: Black-Friday checkouts create 50× the normal number of fulfilment jobs for an hour; the warehouse system can only take a steady rate.
items.why: Every job must eventually be processed, and the burst exceeds a fixed consumer capacity → buffer in a queue (load levelling). Rejecting orders is unacceptable.

items.prompt: A webhook consumer occasionally crashes after charging a card but before acknowledging the message, so customers get charged twice.
items.why: Duplicate processing from at-least-once redelivery → make the consumer idempotent (dedupe by message id). That's a delivery-semantics fix.

items.prompt: The home page must show each user's top 10 search suggestions within 50 ms; the suggestions are recomputed hourly and read millions of times.
items.why: The user needs the answer now, synchronously, so a queue is the wrong tool. Repeated reads of slowly changing data → serve them from a cache.

items.prompt: Five teams each want every 'order placed' event, and a new analytics team needs to reprocess the last 7 days.
items.why: Many independent consumers plus replay → a retained event log with one consumer group per team.
